extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of digital media, memetics, and political communication (and practitioners/activists interested in memetic politics)
extracted.subtask_description: Survey and analysis of major Internet meme genres and the roles memes play in cultural and political participation, including genre-defining features, audience dynamics, and political functions. Useful for researchers, teachers, and practitioners studying or producing memes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lipdub characteristics and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipdubs ... embody a blend of fame and anonymity that characterize participatory culture; lipdubs are based on the reappropriation of mass-mediated hits, originally performed by professional singers, by small, local communities of amateurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the democratizing potential but also the limit: lipdub 'draws a line between amateur and professional art'—most lipsynchers remain anonymous or are labeled as class B YouTube stars; success is often measured by incorporation into traditional mass media. Example: two types of lipdub (frivolous/corporate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misheard-lyrics (phonetic translation) genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Phonetic translation or misheard-lyrics videos are based on amusing mistranslations of spoken sounds to written words, transcribing what the words sound like regardless of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgenres include early 'animutations' (Neil Cicierega's work) and later subtitle-insertion subgenres like 'buffalax' (e.g., 'Benny Lava'). Targets include songs from various languages; examples illustrate globalized linguistic dyads and English songs translated phonetically into other languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recut trailer definition and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A recut trailer is a user-generated 'fake' movie trailer based on the re-editing or remixing of film footage, often displacing the original film's genre to create a radically different movie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodies formulaic marketing strategies by altering narration/patching incongruous music/voice (e.g., The Shining as family comedy). Reflects ambivalent audience relationship with pop culture: mocks marketing while demonstrating digital users' power. Also promotes creators' image as talented/digitally literate.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOLCats: format and social function
rubrics_metrics.description: LOLCats are pictures of cats accompanied by systematically misspelled captions (LOLspeak) that typically refer to the situation shown in the photo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience broken into CheezFrenz (cat lovers), MemeGeeks (genre-aware participants), and casual users; LOLCats construct and maintain social boundaries—enjoyment and creation require familiarity with the genre and its dialect, and they often serve interpersonal communicative functions beyond mere amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock character macros: defining features
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock character macros use image macros and a set of stock characters that represent stereotypical behaviors (e.g., 'Scumbag Steve,' 'Good Guy Greg,' 'Success Kid').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They build on a conceptual map of exaggerated social types and tend to focus on success/failure in social life. The genre originated with 'Advice Dog' and expanded to many derivatives; stock characters encode moral/dramatic templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rage comics: format, characters, and literacy requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rage comics are amateur-looking comics featuring 'rage faces'—a set of expressive characters, each associated with a typical behavior (e.g., Forever Alone, Troll Face, Poker Face).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although technically easy to create (Rage Makers), participation requires subcultural literacy: knowledge of many characters and socially appropriate ways to use them. The genre's narratives often focus on 'Fail', 'WTF', and 'Win' themes, with many strips ending in personal failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-group taxonomy of meme genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Meme genres can be divided into three groups: (1) genres based on documentation of 'real-life' moments (photo fads, flash mobs); (2) genres based on explicit manipulation of visual/audiovisual mass-mediated content ('remix' memes like reaction Photoshops, lipdubs, misheard lyrics, recut trailers); (3) genres evolved around digital/meme-oriented content (LOLCats, rage comics, stock character macros).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group (1) is anchored in nondigital space; group (2) reappropriates news/pop culture and reveals ambivalent attitudes toward pop culture; group (3) requires mastery of a meme subculture and emergent signs/codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as persuasion (political virals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes (and virals) can function as forms of persuasion or political advocacy in campaigns and public debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: many viral campaign clips were posted by traditional actors, but view counts are biased toward nontraditional actors (citizen-designed ads and smaller groups often gain more views). Successful persuasive virals often combine appealing content with distribution support (campaign embrace, bloggers, elite attention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as grassroots action / connective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes serve as grassroots action under the logic of 'connective action'—personalized content sharing across media networks that empowers coordinated action without strong formal organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memes provide shared slogans that are easily personalized and adapted by individuals (e.g., 'Put People First', 'We Are the 99 Percent'), linking personal stories to collective causes and enabling large-scale fluid mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as modes of expression and public discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Meme creation is an accessible, cheap, and enjoyable route for voicing political opinions, producing polyvocal spaces where multiple opinions and identities are negotiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memes accompany major events with a flux of commentary; they can be humorous or serious but aim to make a point and engage in normative debate about how the world should look.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and dynamics of political virality
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all viral political content is produced by lone citizens; a large share of viewership often accrues to content produced by nontraditional but well-resourced actors (interest groups, small media companies), and a small group of 'elite' blogs often ignites viral diffusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies of 2008 campaign videos: party-sponsored ads averaged ~55k views, candidate-sponsored ~60k, interest-group ~139k, citizen-designed ~807k, other entities ~2.5M+. Elite and top-general blogs 'crown' videos and trigger wider blogosphere attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors enhancing spreadability of political memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Spreadability is enhanced by association with influential actors (campaign embracement, bloggers), professional aesthetics, and existing networks that amplify content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Yes We Can' combined celebrity participation, professional production, and campaign endorsement/blog/media attention, which elevated its spread and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic dimensions: form, content, and stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes have three memetic dimensions—form, content, and stance—that reinforce each other to produce persuasive/memetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'We Are the 99 Percent' meme used similar amateur aesthetic (form), personal stories of hardship (content), and a collective stance that framed personal miseries as systemic problems; the alignment of these dimensions increases rhetorical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition + variation and personalization as rhetorical affordances
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of repetition and variation along with personalization turns the personal into the political and strengthens memetic rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: repeated visual/formatal cues (e.g., people holding handwritten signs) create recognizability; varied personal stories provide relatable instances that generalize to systemic critique when framed together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic photos: frontstage/backstage interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Political memetic photos often relate to an interplay between the 'frontstage' and 'backstage' of political performances (Goffman's terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memetic photos typically highlight contrasts between politicians' public image (frontstage) and private/informal moments (backstage), using that tension to critique or reframe political actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pop culture imagery in political memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Pop culture images are used as common ground and shorthand to communicate political meaning (e.g., Star Wars characters denote 'good' vs 'evil').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: increases approachability and shared references; risk: can depoliticize content by privileging playfulness over critical substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcultural literacy as participation barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain meme genres (especially those emerging after ~2007) require mastery of specific signs, codes, and dialects (e.g., LOLspeak, rage-face repertoires), creating in-group knowledge barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: digital literacy alone is insufficient—users need subcultural literacy to produce and be understood within those meme subcultures; this constructs social boundaries and insider/outsider distinctions.
